voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses. Read the quoted email lines flatly, as text on a page, not as a performance.

beats.vo: We sincerely apologize for our actions. I would not want to harm your business, but we have no other choice. An email to Bludorn, a Houston restaurant. July, twenty twenty-two.
The week after the Fourth of July, one-star ratings had appeared on its Google page. No words attached. In one week, four point eight fell to four point five.
The email said there would be one review a day. To stop it: a seventy-five dollar Google Play gift card. Resold, the note said, the card meant three weeks of income for the sender's family.
Google at first said the ratings broke no policy, because there were no comments. The owners didn't pay. They posted the email. About a hundred customers answered with reviews.
When Google finally removed the fake ratings, most of the real five-star reviews went too. The rating settled at four point six.

The apology was a form letter. The New York Times reported the text was the same in each email, sent to restaurants from San Francisco to New York. One-star ratings with no words. And a gift card, because, one consultant said, such transactions are difficult to trace.
